source.title: Beyond Synthetic Noise: Deep Learning on Controlled Noisy Labels
source.authors: Lu Jiang; Di Huang; Mason Liu; Weilong Yang

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present. The text contains minor apparent extraction typos, but the relevant findings are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains vanilla deep networks on controlled synthetic symmetric label noise and measures validation performance and the peak-to-final accuracy drop. It tests related noisy-label behavior, but does not run fully random labels or noise levels above 80%.
record.gate_note: The study's own results test training on up to 80% synthetic label noise and compare with controlled web-label noise. It does not report an exact result for fully random labels, shuffled or Gaussian inputs, training time, or the effect of regularization on fully random labels. Results comparing the proposed MentorMix method with baselines are not cataloged as claim results.
record.test_reason: The study tests the generalization-degradation component of V4 using synthetic label corruption and makes a specific, empirically grounded qualification of V6 using web noise. Its peak-to-final validation gap is indirect evidence of learning order, not a direct measurement of noisy-label memorization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the relevant conclusions: synthetic noise reproduces worsening generalization and validation gaps consistent with early pattern learning; web noise is less damaging and produces smaller gaps, especially on Stanford Cars. The authors tentatively question whether patterns are learned first under web noise and suggest early stopping may help less. These are proxy-based interpretations, not direct demonstrations of learning order.
record.recipe_differences: Vanilla training follows the controlled synthetic label-noise approach, but compares synthetic noise with controlled web noise, uses different datasets and architectures, and tests levels only through 80%.
record.method_sensitivity: The results differ by noise type (synthetic versus web), dataset (Mini-ImageNet versus Stanford Cars), and training setup (from scratch versus fine-tuning); the pattern-learning gap is near zero on Stanford Cars with web noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation performance degrades less under controlled web-image replacement than under synthetic random-label corruption.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization under label noise depends on the noise distribution and image source; controlled web noise can be less damaging than synthetic symmetric noise.

record.problems: The relevant plots do not provide exact values in the text. Noise levels stop at 80%, and the pattern-learning conclusion relies on a peak-to-final validation accuracy gap as an indirect indicator.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported outcomes omitted. The study's training-accuracy curves are shown in Figure 2 but the text gives no separable numeric training-fit results for fully random labels.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and fitting that condition without changing architecture or hyperparameters.
Time to fit true versus random labels and convergence slowdown as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The 100% corruption endpoint, perfect training fit throughout the corruption range, and direct evidence that remaining signal is captured while noise is memorized. Supplied figure text does not establish exact training-fit values.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent fitting completely random labels and whether removing them alone causes poor clean-label generalization.

Direct, separate trajectories for fitting correctly and incorrectly labeled examples, and a completely random-label comparison. Validation gaps alone do not identify the timing of noisy-label memorization.

missing.locator: Supplementary Appendix C, settings 1 and 2, Figure 3 and accompanying discussion

record.verdict_notes: No original-source exclusion applies. Publication is ICML 2020, not 2019. Main Figure 2 panels distinguish datasets and training settings, not red versus blue noise. Appendix B specifies vanilla training without dropout, conflicting with the main baseline description; do not assume dropout was enabled in these experiments. Missing measurements are listed as untested rather than treated as evidence limiting a claim.

versions.untested_parts: No 100% randomly labeled training set or explicit result that vanilla networks fit completely random labels; zero or near-zero training error and test error at chance are not reported for that condition.
Training time to fit random labels and convergence slowdown as corruption rises are not measured.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.

Corruption levels stop at 80%; the study does not establish perfect training-set fit at every level. It reports validation accuracy and its variation across noise levels, rather than test error or proof that the remaining signal is captured while noise is memorized.

The method comparison includes regularization methods on partially corrupted labels, but does not test whether they prevent fitting fully random labels or whether removing them alone harms generalization on true labels.

The study compares synthetic and web label noise, not a direct comparison of real labels with completely random labels. Its peak-to-final validation accuracy gap is an indirect measure of learning patterns before memorization.

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Vanilla training on controlled synthetic symmetric label noise, with clean validation evaluation.
rows.measure: Clean validation accuracy across noise levels; authors report a palpable degradation from 0% to 40% noise and a wider confidence interval across the 10 levels.
rows.value: At 40% noise, the blue validation curve shows a palpable performance degradation; exact figure values are figure only.
rows.note: The text describes the validation result but gives no exact plotted values. This measures generalization degradation, not perfect training fit.
rows.check: The measured degradation component is observed; unmeasured perfect training fit does not make it partial. Supplementary Table 5 supplies exact final validation accuracies: 72.8% at 0%, 43.5% at 40%, and 14.0% at 80% synthetic noise.

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Vanilla training on controlled web label noise, with clean validation evaluation.
rows.measure: Clean validation accuracy across noise levels; authors say the difference between clean and 40% noise is much smaller than for blue noise.
rows.value: At 40% noise, the red validation curve has a much smaller difference from clean than the blue curve; exact figure values are figure only.
rows.note: This is a stated comparison of validation performance, not a measurement of training-set fit.
rows.check: Web noise replaces images with incorrectly labeled web images; it does not randomly corrupt labels as V4 specifies. Figure 2(b) is Mini-ImageNet fine-tuning, not the red-noise panel for training from scratch; the relevant panel is Figure 2(a).

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Vanilla training on controlled synthetic symmetric label noise, with clean validation evaluation.
rows.measure: Standard deviation of final validation accuracies across 10 noise levels.
rows.note: The authors treat higher standard deviation across noise levels as poorer generalization. This does not establish training-set fit.
rows.check: The reported 0.347 standard deviation is correct, but dispersion across noise levels cannot establish the direction or smoothness of degradation. Supplementary Table 7 provides the needed ordered accuracies.

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Vanilla training on controlled web label noise, with clean validation evaluation.
rows.measure: Standard deviation of final validation accuracies across 10 noise levels.
rows.note: The authors treat higher standard deviation across noise levels as poorer generalization; red noise has lower variation than blue noise.
rows.check: The 0.146 value and 0.347 comparison are correct, but web-image replacement does not measure V4's random-label corruption. Standard deviation also cannot establish a steadily worsening trend.

rows.subject: Inception-ResNet-v2
rows.operation_detail: Vanilla training; compare peak and final clean-validation accuracy across noise levels.
rows.measure: Relative drop from peak to final clean-validation accuracy as noise rises.
rows.value: The blue curves show a significant drop as noise level grows; exact plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The authors use a larger peak-to-final validation drop as evidence of patterns being learned early. This is indirect evidence about learning order.
rows.check: Observed as the authors' indirect indicator only. Supplementary Table 5 supplies exact peak/final accuracies: 56.9/43.5% at 40% synthetic noise and 44.6/26.0% at 60%. The gap does not directly establish when noisy labels are memorized.
